case_info.scenario: A 30-year-old nulliparous woman with migraines, depression, and obesity (12.7-kg [28-lb] weight gain over the prior 2 years) presented to the primary care clinic with 1 month of daily headaches, transient bilateral blurry vision, and persistent vision loss in the temporal region of the right eye. She experienced right-sided temporal and frontal headaches accompanied by intermittent auditory hissing, without auras. The headaches lasted for several hours each day, worsened when she was lying flat, and were temporarily relieved by acetaminophen. She took no daily medications or supplements but had a contraceptive etonogestrel implant that had been placed 9 months prior to presentation. Her temperature was 37.1 °C (98.8 °F); heart rate, 95/min; blood pressure, 106/70 mm Hg; height, 1.57 m (5 ft 2 in); weight, 113.9 kg (251 lb); and body mass index, 45 (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in meters). Her pupillary reflexes were brisk bilaterally, without a relative afferent pupillary defect. By visual field testing to confrontation, she had a temporal visual field defect in the right eye. Her physical examination findings were otherwise normal. The patient was referred for same-day ophthalmology evaluation, which revealed visual acuity of 20/20 bilaterally and normal extraocular movements without nystagmus or ocular misalignment. Mild bilateral papilledema was seen on dilated fundoscopy (Figure). Automated visual field testing demonstrated enlargement of the physiologic (temporal) blind spot in the right eye and mild constriction of the left nasal visual field.

case_info.explanation: A. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that symptoms of positional headache, visual blurring, and pulsatile tinnitus are characteristic of IIH in a female with obesity. Lumbar puncture (choice B) should not be performed until neuroimaging has confirmed absence of an intracranial lesion causing papilledema. Prednisone (choice C) is incorrect because the patient’s symptoms were not characteristic of optic neuritis or temporal arteritis. Removal of the birth control implant (choice D) is not recommended because there is no known association between hormonal contraception and IIH.1 IIH is a condition of elevated intracranial pressure without a known cause. It is diagnosed using the modified Dandy criteria, which include (1) symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure such as headache, tinnitus, diplopia, and/or visual disturbances without secondary etiologies (eg, intracranial tumors, venous sinus thrombosis, infection, or medications such as vitamin A derivatives, tetracyclines, lithium, and human growth hormone); (2) papilledema on fundus examination; and (3) elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure on lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position (opening pressure >25 cm H2O in adults; >28 cm H2O in children). IIH primarily affects women of childbearing age and is strongly associated with obesity.2A cross-sectional study of 85 million US patients reported that the prevalence of IIH increased from 7.3 individuals per 100 000 in 2015 to 9.9 per 100 000 in 2022,3correlating with increasing US obesity rates. The pathogenesis of IIH is unclear but may involve hypersecretion and/or decreased absorption of cerebrospinal fluid related to increased levels of androgens, glucocorticoids, glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), and inflammatory cytokines associated with central adiposity.4 First-line treatment for IIH is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (eg, acetazolamide), which causes a rapid reduction of intracranial pressure through decreased cerebrospinal fluid production. Patients with suspected IIH may be treated with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor before confirmation of papilledema, if ophthalmologic examination cannot be not performed expeditiously. If brain MRI/MRV shows no intracranial lesions, patients with suspected IIH should undergo a diagnostic lumbar puncture to determine if cerebrospinal fluid pressure is elevated. While lumbar puncture temporarily decreases intracranial pressure by removing cerebrospinal fluid and may relieve IIH symptoms in the short term, it is not definitive therapy. The combination of a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and weight loss (5%-10%) is effective at improving peripheral vision, papilledema, and vision-related quality-of-life measures.5Small randomized trials of bariatric surgery and a GLP-1 receptor agonist (exenatide) in patients with IIH have demonstrated decreased intracranial pressure compared with control patients.6,7Patients with IIH and fulminant vision loss, or those whose symptoms do not improve or worsen despite medical therapy, may require emergent ventriculoperitoneal shunting, optic nerve sheath fenestration, or venous sinus stenting, although evidence for efficacy of surgical options is lacking.8 The visual prognosis of patients with IIH depends on papilledema grade and visual symptom severity at diagnosis.9,10Untreated IIH can lead to permanent vision loss within several weeks, so early symptom recognition and treatment are important to avoid blindness. Serial ophthalmologic evaluation every 1 to 3 months with quantitative optical coherence tomography and automated visual field testing is indicated for all patients with IIH who have papilledema to evaluate response to therapy and guide treatment. Brain MRI/MRV performed on the day of presentation revealed no intracranial abnormalities but demonstrated diminutive transverse venous sinuses and prominent optic nerve sheath fluid bilaterally, suggestive of elevated intracranial pressure. Same-day lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position revealed a cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure of 33 cm H2O (reference, ≤25 cm H2O); examination of the cerebrospinal fluid showed normal levels of glucose and total protein and no pleocytosis. The patient was prescribed acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and was encouraged to exercise and make dietary modifications. At 1-month follow-up, she reported near-complete resolution of visual blurring and headaches and had lost 2.27 kg (5 lb). Ophthalmologic examination revealed no residual disc edema or visual field defects. She was advised to continue acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and to continue weight loss efforts.

Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that symptoms of positional headache, visual blurring, and pulsatile tinnitus are characteristic of IIH in a female with obesity. Lumbar puncture (choice B) should not be performed until neuroimaging has confirmed absence of an intracranial lesion causing papilledema. Prednisone (choice C) is incorrect because the patient’s symptoms were not characteristic of optic neuritis or temporal arteritis. Removal of the birth control implant (choice D) is not recommended because there is no known association between hormonal contraception and IIH.1 IIH is a condition of elevated intracranial pressure without a known cause. It is diagnosed using the modified Dandy criteria, which include (1) symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure such as headache, tinnitus, diplopia, and/or visual disturbances without secondary etiologies (eg, intracranial tumors, venous sinus thrombosis, infection, or medications such as vitamin A derivatives, tetracyclines, lithium, and human growth hormone); (2) papilledema on fundus examination; and (3) elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure on lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position (opening pressure >25 cm H2O in adults; >28 cm H2O in children). IIH primarily affects women of childbearing age and is strongly associated with obesity.2A cross-sectional study of 85 million US patients reported that the prevalence of IIH increased from 7.3 individuals per 100 000 in 2015 to 9.9 per 100 000 in 2022,3correlating with increasing US obesity rates. The pathogenesis of IIH is unclear but may involve hypersecretion and/or decreased absorption of cerebrospinal fluid related to increased levels of androgens, glucocorticoids, glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), and inflammatory cytokines associated with central adiposity.4 First-line treatment for IIH is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (eg, acetazolamide), which causes a rapid reduction of intracranial pressure through decreased cerebrospinal fluid production. Patients with suspected IIH may be treated with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor before confirmation of papilledema, if ophthalmologic examination cannot be not performed expeditiously. If brain MRI/MRV shows no intracranial lesions, patients with suspected IIH should undergo a diagnostic lumbar puncture to determine if cerebrospinal fluid pressure is elevated. While lumbar puncture temporarily decreases intracranial pressure by removing cerebrospinal fluid and may relieve IIH symptoms in the short term, it is not definitive therapy. The combination of a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and weight loss (5%-10%) is effective at improving peripheral vision, papilledema, and vision-related quality-of-life measures.5Small randomized trials of bariatric surgery and a GLP-1 receptor agonist (exenatide) in patients with IIH have demonstrated decreased intracranial pressure compared with control patients.6,7Patients with IIH and fulminant vision loss, or those whose symptoms do not improve or worsen despite medical therapy, may require emergent ventriculoperitoneal shunting, optic nerve sheath fenestration, or venous sinus stenting, although evidence for efficacy of surgical options is lacking.8 The visual prognosis of patients with IIH depends on papilledema grade and visual symptom severity at diagnosis.9,10Untreated IIH can lead to permanent vision loss within several weeks, so early symptom recognition and treatment are important to avoid blindness. Serial ophthalmologic evaluation every 1 to 3 months with quantitative optical coherence tomography and automated visual field testing is indicated for all patients with IIH who have papilledema to evaluate response to therapy and guide treatment. At 1-month follow-up, she reported near-complete resolution of visual blurring and headaches and had lost 2.27 kg (5 lb).
